stem: Which two structures make up the central nervous system (CNS)?
explanation: The CNS is the brain plus the spinal cord; everything outside them (nerves, ganglia, receptors) is the peripheral nervous system.

stem: Which neuroglial cells form the myelin sheath around axons in the central nervous system?
explanation: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells do the same job in the PNS.

stem: What is the main job of microglia?
option_c: Phagocytizing microbes and cellular debris in the CNS
option_d: Lining the ventricles and forming cerebrospinal fluid
explanation: Microglia are the CNS's cleanup crew; they engulf (phagocytize) microbes and debris, like tiny janitors.

stem: A drug circulates freely in a patient's blood but cannot reach brain tissue. Which neuroglial cells help form the barrier that is most likely blocking it?
explanation: Astrocytes help form the blood-brain barrier, which keeps many substances in the blood from passing into the brain.

stem: Which part of the brainstem contains the cardiovascular center and the respiratory center?
explanation: The medulla oblongata houses vital centers that regulate heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing.

stem: Why does white matter look white?
option_a: It is made mostly of neuron cell bodies
option_b: It is made mostly of myelinated axons
option_c: It is filled with cerebrospinal fluid
option_d: It is made mostly of unmyelinated dendrites
explanation: Myelin is made of lipid (fat) and protein, and that fatty coating gives myelinated axons their white color; gray matter is unmyelinated.

stem: What is the correct order of the meninges from outermost to innermost?
option_a: Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
option_b: Pia mater, arachnoid mater, dura mater
option_c: Arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater
option_d: Dura mater, pia mater, arachnoid mater
explanation: The tough dura mater is outermost, the web-like arachnoid is in the middle, and the delicate pia mater hugs the brain and spinal cord.

stem: A doctor performs a lumbar puncture (spinal tap) to collect a sample of cerebrospinal fluid. Into which space must the needle reach?
explanation: CSF circulates in the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid and pia mater, so that is where a lumbar puncture draws fluid. The epidural space is where pain medication is given.

stem: Where is cerebrospinal fluid produced?
option_c: Gray matter of the spinal cord
option_d: Choroid plexuses in the walls of the ventricles
explanation: Choroid plexuses (capillary networks in the ventricle walls) produce CSF; it is later reabsorbed into the blood.

stem: An infant has an enlarged head, and imaging shows swollen brain ventricles under high pressure. Which explanation best fits these findings?
option_a: The meninges are inflamed by an infection (meningitis)
option_b: Myelin in the brain is being destroyed by the immune system
option_c: The choroid plexuses have stopped producing cerebrospinal fluid
option_d: Cerebrospinal fluid is not draining properly (hydrocephalus)
explanation: In hydrocephalus, CSF keeps being made but cannot drain, so it builds up in the ventricles like water behind a blocked drain.

stem: How many pairs of spinal nerves branch off the spinal cord?
explanation: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves (compared with 12 pairs of cranial nerves).

stem: A neck injury damages a patient's phrenic nerve, and the patient has trouble breathing because the diaphragm is affected. From which plexus does the phrenic nerve branch?
explanation: The phrenic nerve comes off the cervical plexus in the neck and travels down to the diaphragm.

stem: A student says, "Tracts are found in your arms and legs, and nerves are found in your brain." Which correction is accurate?
option_a: Tracts are bundles of axons in the CNS, while nerves are bundles of axons in the PNS
option_b: Tracts and nerves are the same thing and are found only in the PNS
option_c: Tracts are collections of cell bodies in the PNS, while nerves are collections of cell bodies in the CNS
option_d: Nerves are found only in the spinal cord, while tracts are found only in the brain
explanation: The student has it backwards: bundles of axons are called tracts inside the CNS and nerves out in the PNS.

stem: The dorsal root ganglion is a swelling beside the spinal cord that contains the cell bodies of sensory neurons. Because it is a cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS, it is classified as a:
explanation: A ganglion is a collection of neuron cell bodies in the PNS; a similar cluster inside the CNS is called a nucleus.

stem: After a brain injury, a patient staggers when walking, has slurred speech, and cannot coordinate muscle movements smoothly (ataxia). Which brain region was most likely damaged?
explanation: The cerebellum coordinates complex movements, posture, and balance, so damage there causes ataxia.

stem: Neuroglia are smaller and more numerous than neurons.
explanation: True. Neuroglia are smaller and outnumber neurons, making up about half the volume of the CNS.

stem: The epidural space is the space between the dura mater and the vertebral canal, and it is where pain medication can be given.
explanation: True. The epidural space lies outside the dura mater around the spinal cord, which is why an epidural injection can block pain during childbirth.

stem: Because damaged neurons in the CNS repair themselves more easily than those in the PNS, spinal cord injuries usually heal completely.
explanation: False. It is the reverse: PNS neurons have a limited ability to repair, but CNS neurons essentially do not repair, so spinal cord injuries usually cause permanent loss.

stem: Which of the following are part of the peripheral nervous system (PNS)? Select all that apply.
explanation: The PNS includes everything outside the brain and spinal cord, such as cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and ganglia; the spinal cord and cerebellum belong to the CNS.

stem: Which of the following are functions of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)? Select all that apply.
option_a: Absorbing shock to protect the brain and spinal cord
option_c: Providing an optimal chemical environment for synapses
option_d: Exchanging nutrients and wastes with nervous tissue
explanation: CSF cushions the CNS like a water jacket, keeps the chemical environment right for synapses, and exchanges nutrients and wastes; it does not make myelin or carry impulses.

stem: Where is the primary somatosensory area (which receives touch sensations) located?
option_a: Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
option_c: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
explanation: The primary somatosensory area is in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe, just behind the central sulcus.

stem: Where is the primary motor area, which initiates voluntary movements, located?
option_a: Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
option_b: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
option_d: Superior part of the temporal lobe
explanation: The primary motor area is in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe, just in front of the central sulcus.

stem: After a stroke in the left frontal lobe, a patient understands what people say but struggles to form spoken words. Which area was most likely damaged?
explanation: Broca's area, usually in the left frontal lobe, controls the muscle movements of speech; damage causes aphasia, trouble producing speech.

stem: A hard blow to the back of the head damages a patient's primary visual area. Which lobe was injured?
explanation: The primary visual area is in the occipital lobe at the back of the brain.

stem: Which pairing of a cortical area with its lobe is correct?
explanation: Hearing is processed in the temporal lobe, near the ears; the other pairings place each area in the wrong lobe.

stem: Which spinal cord tracts carry pain and temperature sensations to the brain?
explanation: Spinothalamic tracts are ascending sensory tracts that carry pain and temperature information.

stem: With his eyes closed, a patient cannot tell where his fingers are positioned and has trouble feeling light touch, but he can still feel pain and temperature normally. Which tracts are most likely damaged?
explanation: Posterior column tracts carry touch and proprioception, while spinothalamic tracts (still working here) carry pain and temperature.

stem: What do the direct (pyramidal) tracts carry?
option_a: Nerve impulses for unconscious, automatic movements
option_b: Pain and temperature information to the brain
option_c: Touch and proprioception information to the brain
option_d: Nerve impulses for voluntary movements of skeletal muscles
explanation: Direct (pyramidal) tracts are descending motor tracts for voluntary, conscious movements such as writing.

stem: A stroke damages the primary motor area in the LEFT cerebral hemisphere, and the patient's RIGHT arm becomes weak. Which fact best explains this?
option_a: Most motor tracts cross to the opposite side in the medulla oblongata (decussation of pyramids)
option_b: The right hemisphere controls language and reasoning
option_c: Sensory tracts cross over in the cerebellum
option_d: Spinal nerves from the left side of the cord supply the right arm
explanation: Motor tracts cross over at the decussation of pyramids in the medulla, so each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.

stem: What is the main role of the thalamus in sensory processing?
option_a: It regulates heart rate and blood pressure
option_b: It produces hormones and controls the pituitary gland
option_c: It coordinates balance and smooth movement
option_d: It is the main relay station that sends sensory information on to the cerebral cortex
explanation: The thalamus works like a switchboard, sorting incoming sensory signals and relaying them to the correct area of the cortex.

stem: What kind of information does the dorsal (posterior) root of a spinal nerve carry?
option_b: Signals between the two cerebral hemispheres
option_c: Cerebrospinal fluid into the central canal
option_d: Sensory information into the spinal cord
explanation: The dorsal root carries sensory information into the cord; the ventral root carries motor information out.

stem: A patient has a resting tremor, stiff (rigid) muscles, and trouble starting and stopping movements. Damage to which structure best explains these symptoms?
explanation: The basal ganglia start and stop movements, suppress unwanted movements, and regulate muscle tone; their damage causes the tremors and rigidity of Parkinson's disease.

stem: What is the main function of the association areas of the cerebral cortex?
option_a: To send motor impulses directly to skeletal muscles
option_b: To integrate and interpret information, store memories, and contribute to personality and intelligence
option_c: To receive raw sensory signals directly from receptors in the skin
option_d: To produce cerebrospinal fluid for the ventricles
explanation: Association areas sit next to the primary areas and make sense of the information, for example recognizing that a pattern of light is a friend's face.

stem: A paper cut stimulates receptors that warn the body of tissue damage. Which type of receptor is this?
explanation: Nociceptors detect pain, which acts as a warning sign of tissue damage.

stem: Meissner corpuscles (touch) and Pacinian corpuscles (pressure) are examples of which type of receptor?
explanation: Mechanoreceptors detect mechanical forces such as touch, pressure, and vibration that physically deform the receptor.

stem: In most people, the left cerebral hemisphere is more important for language, math, and reasoning, while the right hemisphere is more involved in musical, artistic, and spatial skills.
explanation: True. This is called hemispheric lateralization; each hemisphere specializes in certain tasks.

stem: Indirect (extrapyramidal) tracts carry nerve impulses for conscious, voluntary movements such as writing your name.
explanation: False. Indirect (extrapyramidal) tracts carry impulses for unconscious, automatic movements such as posture; direct (pyramidal) tracts handle voluntary movements.

stem: Receptors detect a stimulus and create nerve impulses, but conscious awareness of the stimulus (perception) does not happen until the impulses reach the cerebral cortex.
explanation: True. A receptor only starts the signal; you become aware of a sensation when it is processed in the cerebral cortex.

stem: Which of the following are general somatic senses? Select all that apply.
explanation: Somatic senses (touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain, proprioception) have receptors spread throughout the body; vision and hearing are special senses.

stem: Which statements correctly describe the motor pathway for a voluntary movement, such as kicking a ball? Select all that apply.
option_a: It travels down the spinal cord in the ascending tracts
option_b: It begins in the primary motor area of the precentral gyrus
option_c: Most of its axons cross to the opposite side in the medulla oblongata
option_d: It leaves the spinal cord through the ventral root to reach skeletal muscle
explanation: Voluntary motor signals start in the precentral gyrus, cross in the medulla, descend in descending (not ascending) tracts, and exit through the ventral root to the muscle.

stem: Somatic motor neurons carry impulses to which effectors?
option_d: Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands
explanation: The somatic nervous system controls skeletal muscles only, which is why it is under voluntary control.

stem: The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system is also called the:
explanation: Sympathetic neurons leave the spinal cord in the thoracic and lumbar regions, so it is the thoracolumbar division.

stem: While hiking, a student suddenly sees a bear on the trail. Which response would you expect from the student's autonomic nervous system?
option_a: Heart rate slows and digestion increases
option_c: Blood flow to the digestive tract increases
explanation: The sympathetic "fight or flight" response dilates the pupils to let in more light and the airways to let in more air.

stem: After eating a large Thanksgiving dinner, a person relaxes on the couch. Which division is dominant, and what is one effect?
explanation: The parasympathetic "rest and digest" division dominates when the body is relaxed and boosts digestion.

stem: What does dual innervation mean in the autonomic nervous system?
option_a: Each skeletal muscle is supplied by two motor neurons
option_b: Most organs receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves; one increases activity and the other decreases it
option_c: Every nerve has both sensory and motor axons
option_d: Both the brain and the spinal cord send voluntary signals to each organ
explanation: With dual innervation, the two divisions act like a gas pedal and a brake on the same organ.

stem: Where are the sympathetic trunk ganglia located?
option_a: On each side of the vertebral column
option_b: In or near the walls of the organs they control
explanation: Sympathetic trunk ganglia form a chain on each side of the vertebral column; parasympathetic ganglia are usually in or near the organs.

stem: Which sequence correctly describes an autonomic motor pathway?
option_a: Postganglionic neuron in the CNS, then a ganglion, then a preganglionic neuron, then the effector
option_b: A single motor neuron travels from the CNS directly to the effector
option_c: Preganglionic neuron in the CNS, then a ganglion, then a postganglionic neuron, then the effector
option_d: Sensory neuron, then preganglionic neuron, then the brain, then the effector
explanation: Autonomic pathways use two neurons: the preganglionic neuron runs from the CNS to a ganglion, and the postganglionic neuron goes from the ganglion to the muscle or gland.

stem: Which statement correctly compares somatic and autonomic motor pathways?
option_a: Somatic pathways control cardiac and smooth muscle, while autonomic pathways control skeletal muscle
option_b: Somatic pathways are involuntary, while autonomic pathways are voluntary
option_c: Somatic pathways use one motor neuron from the CNS to the effector, while autonomic pathways use two neurons that synapse in a ganglion
option_d: Somatic pathways synapse in sympathetic trunk ganglia, while autonomic pathways do not use ganglia
explanation: A somatic motor neuron runs directly to skeletal muscle (voluntary), while autonomic pathways are involuntary and need a pre- and a postganglionic neuron.

stem: The effects of a sudden fright, such as a pounding heart, often last for minutes after the danger has passed. Which explanation fits best?
option_a: The sympathoadrenal branch stimulated the adrenal glands to release epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood
option_b: The vagus nerve continued to slow the heart
option_c: The parasympathetic division released hormones that speed up the heart
option_d: The hypoglossal nerve kept signaling the heart
explanation: Adrenal hormones travel in the blood and take time to be cleared, so the fight-or-flight effects linger after the nerve signals stop.

stem: How many pairs of cranial nerves are there?
explanation: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves, which branch from the brain and brainstem (versus 31 pairs of spinal nerves).

stem: During a neurological exam, a patient cannot shrug his shoulders or turn his head against resistance. Which cranial nerve is most likely damaged?
explanation: The (spinal) accessory nerve controls the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles, which shrug the shoulders and turn the head.

stem: A patient suddenly cannot smile or close one eye on the left side of her face (Bell's palsy). Which cranial nerve is affected?
explanation: The facial nerve controls the muscles of facial expression; the trigeminal nerve handles facial touch and chewing.

stem: Which cranial nerve carries most of the parasympathetic output to the organs of the chest and abdomen?
explanation: The vagus ("wandering") nerve travels far beyond the head to the heart, lungs, and digestive organs, carrying parasympathetic signals.

stem: A patient's right eye cannot turn outward (laterally), but it can still move up, down, and inward. Which cranial nerve is most likely damaged?
explanation: The abducens nerve controls the muscle that abducts (moves outward) the eye; the oculomotor nerve, which still works here, handles most other eye movements.

stem: Which brain structure is the major control center for the autonomic nervous system?
explanation: The hypothalamus controls the ANS, helping regulate heart rate, body temperature, hunger, and thirst.

stem: The enteric nervous system is under involuntary control and controls the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
explanation: True. The enteric nervous system is the "brain of the gut"; it works involuntarily to control the GI tract.

stem: Parasympathetic ganglia are usually located in or near the walls of the organs they control.
explanation: True. Parasympathetic ganglia are terminal ganglia close to their organs, unlike the sympathetic trunk ganglia beside the vertebral column.

stem: Because the vagus nerve is a cranial nerve, it serves only structures in the head and neck.
explanation: False. Even though it starts in the brainstem, the vagus nerve travels down into the chest and abdomen to supply organs like the heart, lungs, and intestines.

stem: Which of the following are effects of sympathetic stimulation? Select all that apply.
option_d: Constriction of blood vessels to the skin and GI tract
explanation: Fight-or-flight speeds the heart, increases sweating, and shunts blood away from nonessential organs; salivation and pupil constriction are parasympathetic effects.

stem: Taste information travels to the brain on three different cranial nerves. Which cranial nerves carry taste? Select all that apply.
explanation: The facial, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves carry taste; the hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue but does not carry taste, and the olfactory nerve carries smell.

stem: Which part of a neuron receives information and carries nerve impulses toward the cell body?
explanation: Dendrites are the branching "antennae" of a neuron that pick up incoming signals and carry them to the cell body.

stem: Which part of a neuron is usually a single long branch that carries nerve impulses away from the cell body to another neuron, muscle, or gland?
explanation: The axon is the neuron's output cable, carrying impulses away from the cell body.

stem: What is the role of interneurons (association neurons)?
option_a: They carry information from sensory receptors to the CNS
option_b: They carry commands from the CNS to muscles and glands
option_c: They form the myelin sheath around axons
option_d: They connect sensory neurons to motor neurons within the CNS and integrate information
explanation: Interneurons sit between sensory and motor neurons in the CNS and are responsible for integration, deciding what to do with incoming information.

stem: Motor neurons are also called:
explanation: Motor neurons are efferent; they carry information away from the CNS (Efferent = Exits). Sensory neurons are afferent (Afferent = Arrives).

stem: Which description matches a neuron at rest (polarized)?
option_a: The inside is negative with more K+, and the outside is positive with more Na+
option_b: The inside is positive with more Na+, and the outside is negative with more K+
option_c: The inside is negative with more Na+, and the outside is positive with more K+
option_d: There is no difference in charge across the membrane
explanation: At rest, the outside of the membrane is positive with more Na+, and the inside is negative with more K+. This charge difference must be maintained to make an impulse.

stem: What causes depolarization during an action potential?
option_a: K+ channels open, and K+ moves out of the cell
option_b: The sodium-potassium pump moves ions back to where they started
option_c: Na+ channels open, and Na+ rushes into the cell
option_d: Neurotransmitter is broken down in the synaptic cleft
explanation: When Na+ channels open, positive sodium ions flood in, and the inside of the cell flips from negative to positive.

stem: What happens during repolarization?
option_a: Na+ channels open, so Na+ rushes in and the inside becomes positive
option_b: Na+ channels close and K+ channels open, so K+ moves out and the inside returns to negative
option_c: K+ channels open, so K+ rushes in and the inside becomes positive
option_d: Neurotransmitter binds receptors and the inside becomes more positive
explanation: Repolarization resets the charge: K+ leaving the cell carries positive charge out, making the inside negative again.

stem: A researcher gives a neuron one stimulus that is below threshold and then a second stimulus that is twice the threshold. What happens?
option_a: No action potential occurs with the weak stimulus, and a normal full-size action potential occurs with the strong stimulus
option_b: A small action potential occurs with the weak stimulus, and a double-size action potential occurs with the strong one
option_c: Both stimuli produce action potentials, but the strong one is larger
option_d: The weak stimulus produces an action potential that fades out before reaching the axon
explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none: below threshold nothing happens, and once threshold is reached the impulse is always the same size, like a light switch that is either off or on.

stem: What is the refractory period?
option_a: The time it takes neurotransmitter to cross the synaptic cleft
option_b: The recovery time needed before another action potential can be generated
option_c: The time it takes the membrane to reach threshold
option_d: The gap between two Schwann cells on an axon
explanation: During the refractory period a neuron is "recharging" and cannot fire another action potential right away.

stem: Why does a myelinated axon conduct nerve impulses faster than an unmyelinated axon of the same size?
option_a: The impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next instead of traveling along every part of the membrane
option_b: Myelin pumps extra Na+ into the axon to strengthen the impulse
option_c: Myelin makes the axon physically shorter
option_d: Unmyelinated axons have no ion channels, so they rely on diffusion
explanation: Myelin insulates the axon, so the impulse leaps between the gaps (nodes of Ranvier), like taking long strides instead of tiny steps.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has episodes of blurred vision and muscle weakness that come and go (relapses and remissions). An MRI shows loss of myelin in her brain and spinal cord. Which disorder best fits?
explanation: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that destroys myelin in the CNS, alternates between relapses and remissions, and affects women about twice as often as men.

stem: Which sequence correctly lists the parts of a reflex arc?
option_a: Receptor, sensory neuron, integrating center, motor neuron, effector
option_b: Receptor, motor neuron, integrating center, sensory neuron, effector
option_c: Effector, sensory neuron, integrating center, motor neuron, receptor
option_d: Sensory neuron, receptor, motor neuron, integrating center, effector
explanation: A reflex arc goes from detecting the stimulus (receptor) to carrying it in (sensory neuron), deciding (integrating center), carrying the command out (motor neuron), and responding (effector).

stem: When a doctor taps the patellar tendon, the quadriceps muscle contracts and the lower leg kicks. In this reflex arc, the quadriceps muscle is the:
explanation: The effector is the muscle or gland that responds; here the quadriceps contracts to produce the kick.

stem: A doctor taps a patient's patellar tendon and gets no response at all. What does an absent reflex most likely indicate?
option_a: A normal result showing the brain is overriding the reflex
option_b: That the patient's quadriceps muscle is unusually strong
option_c: That the receptor is working but responding too quickly to see
option_d: Possible damage or disease somewhere in the nervous system along the reflex pathway
explanation: Reflexes are predictable, so an absent or abnormal reflex is a clue that part of the pathway (nerve, spinal cord, or muscle) may be damaged or diseased.

stem: A drug blocks the receptors on the membrane of a postsynaptic neuron. What is the most likely effect at that synapse?
option_a: The presynaptic neuron can no longer produce action potentials
option_b: The nerve impulse jumps electrically across the synaptic cleft instead
option_c: Neurotransmitter is still released but cannot bind, so the signal is not passed to the postsynaptic neuron
option_d: The postsynaptic neuron releases extra neurotransmitter back toward the presynaptic neuron
explanation: Neurotransmitter must bind receptors like a key in a lock; if the locks are blocked, the message cannot be delivered even though the key is released.

stem: A reflex requires a conscious decision in the cerebral cortex before the effector responds.
explanation: False. A reflex is a fast, automatic, involuntary response; many reflexes are integrated in the spinal cord without waiting for a conscious decision.

stem: After an action potential, the sodium-potassium pump moves Na+ and K+ back to where they started, restoring the resting distribution of ions.
explanation: True. Once the K+ channels close, the sodium-potassium pump resets the ions so the neuron is ready for the next impulse.

stem: Because the gray matter of the spinal cord can act as the integrating center, you can pull your hand away from a hot stove before your brain is consciously aware of the pain.
explanation: True. In a spinal reflex the decision is made in the spinal cord's gray matter, so the response happens before the pain signal finishes traveling up to the brain.

stem: Which of the following are examples of reflexes? Select all that apply.
option_a: Pulling your hand away from a hot stove
option_b: Choosing which song to play next
option_c: Your knee jerking when the patellar tendon is tapped
option_d: Blinking when an object flies toward your eye
explanation: Reflexes are fast, automatic, involuntary responses that usually protect the body; choosing a song or solving a problem requires conscious thought.

stem: Which statements correctly describe a chemical synapse? Select all that apply.
option_a: The presynaptic neuron releases a neurotransmitter
option_b: The nerve impulse jumps directly across the synaptic cleft as electricity
option_c: The two neurons meet but do not physically touch
option_d: The neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron
option_e: The postsynaptic neuron sends the neurotransmitter back to start the impulse
explanation: At a synapse, the presynaptic neuron releases neurotransmitter that crosses the gap and binds receptors on the postsynaptic neuron, because the electrical impulse itself cannot jump the gap.

stem: Which photoreceptors work best in dim light and produce black-and-gray vision?
explanation: Rods are very light-sensitive and work in dim light but do not detect color; cones handle color vision in bright light.

stem: The central fovea is the point of sharpest vision. What type of photoreceptor does it contain?
option_b: Equal numbers of rods and cones
explanation: The central fovea of the macula lutea contains only cones, packed tightly, which is why it gives the sharpest, most detailed vision.

stem: A man has growing trouble seeing at dusk and at night. His doctor suspects a dietary deficiency. Which vitamin deficiency can cause this night blindness?
explanation: Vitamin A is needed to make the light-sensitive pigment in rods, so a deficiency leads to night blindness.

stem: A student can read a book clearly but sees the board at the front of the room as blurry. Where are images of distant objects focusing in the student's eye?
option_d: Unevenly because of an irregular cornea (astigmatism)
explanation: This student is nearsighted (myopia): distant images focus in front of the retina, so far objects look blurry.

stem: Why is there a blind spot in each eye?
option_a: The optic disc, where the optic nerve leaves the eye, has no photoreceptors
option_b: The macula lutea contains only cones
option_c: The choroid blocks light from reaching that part of the retina
option_d: The lens cannot focus light onto that area
explanation: Where the optic nerve exits (the optic disc) there are no rods or cones, so light landing there cannot be detected.

stem: A patient has increased pressure inside the eye that, if untreated, can damage the retina and optic nerve and cause blindness. Which fluid is building up, and what is the condition?
explanation: In glaucoma, aqueous humor in the anterior cavity does not drain properly, so intraocular pressure rises and damages the retina and optic nerve.

stem: A 50-year-old needs reading glasses because the lens of her eye has lost its elasticity with age and no longer focuses well on close objects. What is this condition called?
explanation: Presbyopia is age-related loss of lens elasticity; a cataract, by contrast, is a clouding of the lens.

stem: You look up from a distant mountain to read a text message. Which changes allow your eyes to focus on the close-up screen (accommodation)?
option_a: The cornea flattens, and the pupils dilate
option_b: The iris pulls the retina closer to the lens
option_c: The ciliary muscle changes the lens to a rounder shape, and the pupils constrict
option_d: The vitreous body thickens to bend light more
explanation: For near vision, the ciliary muscle makes the lens rounder so it bends light more, and the pupils constrict to keep the image sharp.

stem: In what order do the auditory ossicles pass vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window?
explanation: The malleus (hammer) touches the eardrum, the incus (anvil) is in the middle, and the stapes (stirrup) pushes on the oval window.

stem: Where are the hair cells that act as receptors for hearing located?
option_a: In the spiral organ (organ of Corti) of the cochlea
explanation: The spiral organ (organ of Corti) inside the snail-shaped cochlea contains the hair cells that turn sound vibrations into nerve impulses.

stem: As an airplane descends, your ears "pop" as the pressure on both sides of your eardrum evens out. Which structure makes this possible?
option_a: The external auditory canal, which connects the outer ear to the eardrum
option_b: The cochlea, which contains fluid-filled chambers
option_c: The auditory (Eustachian) tube, which connects the middle ear to the throat
option_d: The semicircular canals, which detect head movement
explanation: The auditory (Eustachian) tube links the air-filled middle ear to the throat, so swallowing or yawning lets air in or out to equalize pressure.

stem: A figure skater spins rapidly. Which structures of the inner ear detect this rotational movement of the head (dynamic equilibrium)?
explanation: The three semicircular canals detect rotational head movements (dynamic equilibrium); the vestibule handles static equilibrium.

stem: After years of loud concerts, a musician's cochlear hair cells are damaged. What type of hearing loss is this, and which sounds are typically lost first?
explanation: Damage to cochlear hair cells or the vestibulocochlear nerve is sensorineural deafness, and noise or aging usually takes away high-pitched sounds first.

stem: Which sequence describes the olfactory pathway?
option_a: Chemoreceptors in the nose, then optic nerves, then the occipital lobe
option_b: Chemoreceptors in the nose, then olfactory nerves, then the temporal lobe
option_c: Taste buds, then facial nerves, then the parietal lobe
option_d: Chemoreceptors in the nose, then vagus nerves, then the medulla oblongata
explanation: Odor chemicals stimulate chemoreceptors in the nose, the olfactory nerves carry the signal, and it is interpreted in the temporal lobe; links to the limbic system explain why smells trigger memories.

stem: If you dry your tongue with a paper towel and place a few grains of sugar on it, you may taste very little at first. Why?
option_a: Taste buds are mechanoreceptors that need moisture to bend
option_b: Sugar can only be detected by the olfactory receptors
option_c: Taste chemicals must dissolve in saliva before they can stimulate the taste buds
option_d: A dry tongue blocks the hypoglossal nerve
explanation: Taste buds contain chemoreceptors, and chemicals have to be dissolved in saliva to reach and stimulate them.

stem: The iris regulates how much light enters the eye; in bright light, the pupils constrict.
explanation: True. The iris adjusts pupil size like a camera aperture, constricting in bright light and dilating in dim light.

stem: Static equilibrium, which keeps track of head position relative to gravity, is detected mainly by the semicircular canals.
explanation: False. Static equilibrium is detected by the vestibule; the semicircular canals detect rotational movement (dynamic equilibrium).

stem: Because light rays bend (refract) as they pass through the cornea and lens, the image formed on the retina is upside down and reversed, and the brain interprets it so that we see the world right-side up.
explanation: True. Refraction flips the image on the retina, much like a camera lens, and the brain corrects it during processing.

stem: Which of the following are special senses? Select all that apply.
explanation: Special senses (smell, taste, vision, hearing, and balance) have receptors located in one specific area; proprioception and pain are general senses spread throughout the body.

stem: Which structures belong to the vascular tunic (middle layer) of the eyeball? Select all that apply.
explanation: The vascular tunic includes the choroid, ciliary body, and iris; the sclera is part of the outer fibrous tunic, and the retina is the inner layer.
